OnlineMate: An LLM-Based Multi-Agent Companion System for Cognitive Support in Online Learning

Xian Gao Zongyun Zhang    Ting Liu    Yuzhuo Fu
Abstract

In online learning environments, students often lack personalized peer interactions, which play a crucial role in supporting cognitive development and learning engagement. Although previous studies have utilized large language models (LLMs) to simulate interactive dynamic learning environments for students, these interactions remain limited to conversational exchanges, lacking insights and adaptations to the learners’ individualized learning and cognitive states. As a result, students’ interest in discussions with AI learning companions is low, and they struggle to gain inspiration from such interactions. To address this challenge, we propose OnlineMate, a multi-agent learning companion system driven by LLMs that integrates the Theory of Mind (ToM). OnlineMate is capable of simulating peer-like agent roles, adapting to learners’ cognitive states during collaborative discussions, and inferring their psychological states, such as misunderstandings, confusion, or motivation. By incorporating Theory of Mind capabilities, the system can dynamically adjust its interaction strategies to support the development of higher-order thinking and cognition. Experimental results in simulated learning scenarios demonstrate that OnlineMate effectively fosters deep learning and discussions while enhancing cognitive engagement in online educational settings.

1Shanghai Jiao Tong University

gaoxian@sjtu.edu.cn

Introduction

The use of artificial intelligence to provide students with immediate and personalized instruction online traces its origins to the era of Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITS) (Nwana 1990). With the advancement of large language models (LLMs), LLM-driven online AI teachers (Markel et al. 2023) and teaching assistants (Tu et al. 2023) have become widely adopted. However, unlike learning in traditional classrooms, students engaging in online learning through these AI technologies often face the challenge of limited interaction, which results in a weakened sense of classroom participation (Muilenburg and Berge 2005; Ferri, Grifoni, and Guzzo 2020; Akpen et al. 2024).

In an effort to further simulate authentic classroom environments in online teaching settings and enhance students’ interactive experiences, some studies (Yu et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025c) have leveraged the multi-agent collaboration and social simulation capabilities of LLMs (Park et al. 2023; Aher, Arriaga, and Kalai 2023; Li et al. 2023; Guo et al. 2024) to simulate peer companions for students in online learning environments. These approaches aim to stimulate classroom discussions, thereby increasing student interaction and engagement in online learning. However, these methods rely solely on LLMs to adopt specific character roles for dialogue, lacking control over whether the discussion content aligns with students’ needs or whether it can spark students’ interest in participating. Moreover, they fail to initiate targeted, personalized discussions that take into account students’ cognitive levels and psychological states, which would stimulate deeper reflection and enhance cognitive development during discussions.

To address these limitations, we leverage the Theory of Mind (ToM) capabilities of LLMs, which enable the inference of others’ thoughts and psychological states (Apperly 2010) (Zhu, Zhang, and Wang 2024; Nguyen 2025; Zhang et al. 2025b), and propose OnlineMate, a multi-agent learning companion system enhanced by ToM and driven by LLMs. This system not only simulates peer-like agent roles for dialogue but also infers and adapts to learners’ cognitive and psychological states during collaborative discussions, dynamically adjusting its interaction strategies to cater to learners’ interests and needs, thereby enhancing their engagement and fostering cognitive development. We decompose the process by which OnlineMate agents generate responses during student classroom discussions into three stages, in alignment with metacognitive theory (Flavell 1979; Zhang et al. 2025b), which posits that humans infer others’ thoughts, generate their own understanding, and adjust their behavior prior to speaking. Specifically, the OnlineMate agent first generates multiple hypotheses about the student’s cognitive and psychological state based on the context and dialogue content, reflecting the first step of human ToM: interpreting the potential deeper meaning the speaker is attempting to convey through language. For instance, when a student asks, “Why is multi-head attention used in Transformers?”, the OnlineMate agents might infer that the student is struggling with understanding Transformer concepts and is interested in the structure and principles of Transformers. The agent then refines and filters these hypotheses by incorporating real-world factors such as the agent’s persona, knowledge background, and course content. Just as humans refine their initial interpretations based on their own background and the context of the conversation, an agent with an expert persona may interpret the question as an inquiry, whereas an agent modeled as a novice student may perceive it as a need for empathy. Finally, the OnlineMate agent generates and self-validates its output, enabling the system to respond with a more nuanced understanding and answers that align with the student’s expectations.

We conducted a comprehensive evaluation of OnlineMate, which included evaluating the performance of LLM-simulated students within the system (Gao et al. 2024; Anthis et al. 2025; Thapa et al. 2025) and and human evaluations using standardized rubrics to evaluate the quality of simulated student participation in discussions within OnlineMate. The results demonstrated that OnlineMate effectively enhances students’ cognitive levels, providing them with meaningful insights during discussions. Additionally, we performed an in-depth ablation study, revealing the influence of various factors within OnlineMate on student learning outcomes.

Our primary contributions are summarized as follows:

  • •

    We propose OnlineMate, a multi-agent learning companion system enhanced by Theory of Mind (ToM) and driven by LLMs. It infers students’ cognitive and psychological states and dynamically adjusts its interaction strategies to cater to learners’ interests and needs.

  • •

    We conducted a comprehensive evaluation, demonstrating that the proposed OnlineMate can significantly enhance students’ learning outcomes and experiences.

  • •

    We performed an in-depth ablation study to investigate the impact of various factors on student learning outcomes and experiences, providing deeper insights for educational research.

Related Work

LLMs in Education

The pretraining of LLMs on extensive corpora has equipped them with expert-level proficiency across diverse domains. Numerous studies have examined the deployment of LLMs in educational contexts, applying them directly to downstream tasks such as teaching assistance (JeonJaeho and LeeSeongyong 2023), lesson planning (HuBihao et al. 2024), and instructional report generation (Gao et al. 2025a). Other research integrates LLMs into traditional classrooms, employing them to simulate students for training teachers or teaching assistants (Lee et al. 2023; Markel et al. 2023), or to serve as instructors delivering lessons (Tu et al. 2023; Shi, Liang, and Xu 2025). Capitalizing on LLMs’ role-playing capabilities, virtual agents have been designed to support teaching, including orchestrating discussions through multiple student agents (Yue et al. 2025), or simulating both teachers and students via different agents (Zhang et al. 2025c; Yu et al. 2024). However, these approaches lack mechanisms for personalized adaptation, falling short in dynamically tailoring instructional content to individual learners.

LLMs for Human Simulation

Due to the encoding of extensive human behaviors in their training data and preference optimization, LLM-driven agents have demonstrated human-like decision-making and action capabilities across various domains. An increasing number of researchers have begun utilizing LLMs for simulating human scenarios, such as in social and psychological studies (Park et al. 2023; Aher, Arriaga, and Kalai 2023; Li et al. 2023; Guo et al. 2024; Lin et al. 2024), scientific inquiry (M. Bran et al. 2024; Li et al. 2025c; Gao et al. 2025b), and collaborative workflows (Hong et al. 2023; Li et al. 2024; Kulkarni 2025). In the field of education, researchers have explored the feasibility of using LLMs for role-playing to simulate teachers and students in real classroom settings (Zhang et al. 2025c; Yu et al. 2024). However, in these studies, LLMs simulate roles by merely imitating conversational styles, thus still leaving a gap between such simulations and authentic classroom instruction.

Theory of Mind (ToM) in LLMs

Theory of Mind (ToM)—the capacity to attribute mental states to others and anticipate their behavior (Premack and Woodruff 1978)—is a core component of human cognition and social intelligence, enabling inference and prediction of others’ actions (Apperly 2012). Recent research shows that LLMs exhibit notable ToM abilities (van Duijn et al. 2023), with internal representations of self and others’ belief states embedded in their architecture (Zhu, Zhang, and Wang 2024), which critically impact their ToM performance. ToM reasoning, alongside broader social commonsense, has proven essential across AI subfields such as dialogue systems (Kim et al. 2023), complex interactive scenarios (Zhou et al. 2023; Kim et al. 2023), and multimodal question answering (Jin et al. 2024). To strengthen LLMs’ ToM abilities, some studies propose decomposing reasoning into explicit inference chains (Gu et al. 2024b; Lin et al. 2025) or modeling workflows involving multiple agents (Zhang et al. 2025b). In this work, we similarly decompose the ToM reasoning of OnlineMate Agents into three stages to enhance reasoning performance while preserving persona consistency.

OnlineMate Framework

The design of an LLM-agent-based classroom simulation must ensure that (1) each agent’s behavior aligns with its predefined persona and that all agents receive appropriate and accurate contextual information, and (2) interactions throughout the classroom process unfold in a natural and coherent manner. To address the first requirement, we introduce a Classroom Context Manager, which governs the flow of information accessible to each OnlineMate Agent within the framework. For the second, we develop a Classroom Behavior Controller, which determines the actions undertaken by each agent, maintaining the dynamics of interaction in a manner consistent with real classroom environments. Furthermore, to facilitate a more rigorous evaluation of system functionality, we incorporate an evaluation agent tasked with simulating student roles, thereby enabling systematic evaluation of OnlineMate Agents’ pedagogical effectiveness. Figure 1 shows the composition of our proposed framework and its workflow.

Classroom Context Manager

The classroom teaching process represents a multifaceted and information-dense communication environment. During role-playing, LLMs may encounter issues such as hallucinations and role reversals (Park et al. 2023; Qian et al. 2024). Furthermore, within the classroom dialogue, each OnlineMate Agent, in addition to having access to all visible dialogues and discussions, maintains independent contextual memories, inferences, beliefs, and other elements. To manage the contextual content for different OnlineMate Agents, we implement a Classroom Context Manager. In its context database, we store not only the context content ctx and its type type (e.g., dialogue, memory, inference, etc.), but also the corresponding visible range range, such as the ID of a specific OnlineMate Agent, the set of all agents within a discussion group, or all agents in the classroom. To enhance the consistency of role-playing within LLMs, the database also retains each OnlineMate Agent’s role setting as part of the memory. In summary, the attributes of each entry in the context database are (pk, ctx, range, role, type, timestamp). When generating a response, each OnlineMate Agent queries its role setting and visible context from the database, and based on the timestamps, incorporates this information into the LLM’s input, thereby ensuring the independent and efficient management of each OnlineMate Agent’s context.

Classroom Behavior Controller

To ensure that the behavior of OnlineMate Agents remains consistent with their personas and human-like actions, while also preserving the autonomy of the agents’ behaviors, we utilize the Classroom Behavior Controller to govern their actions within the classroom. Specifically, for agents with different roles, we define a set of permissible actions that align with their respective personas. For instance, the possible actions for a teacher role include explain, answer questions, call roll, etc., while actions for an introverted student may include remain silent, speak, ask questions, etc.. When generating responses, the Classroom Behavior Controller provides each agent with its visible context and prompts the agent to assign a score between 0 and 10 to represent the degree of intention behind their decision to speak, with a higher score indicating a stronger determination to take the speaking action. Based on the agents’ intention scores, the Classroom Behavior Controller selects which agent will speak in the current round. To avoid any single agent being overly assertive, the Classroom Behavior Controller is configured to randomly select a speaking agent from the top nn agents based on their intention rankings. The controller then chooses an action from the agent’s respective action list and incorporates the action type as one of the prompts for generating the agent’s response. If an agent’s action pertains to another agent, such as a teacher’s questioning behavior, the agent to take action next will be set as the agent who was referenced.

Evaluation Agent

To mitigate ethical concerns associated with prematurely deploying underdeveloped systems, we adopt the LLM-as-a-judge paradigm (Gu et al. 2024a; Li et al. 2025a), integrating an Evaluation Agent into the OnlineMate framework to evaluate system performance in place of actual student users. Prior research has demonstrated that LLMs can effectively simulate students’ cognitive and emotional states, providing a viable alternative to human experimentation while avoiding associated ethical challenges (Lu and Wang 2024; Li et al. 2025b). Unlike conventional LLM-as-a-judge approaches, which typically evaluate surface-level textual content, the evaluation of OnlineMate necessitates judging the system’s capacity to understand and respond to human cognitive and affective processes. To this end, we augment the Evaluation Agent with mechanisms to simulate affective and cognitive developmental processes, a method that has been empirically shown to yield highly correlated approximations of genuine human psychological responses (Zhang et al. 2025a)11 1 In extensive experiments across 100 supportive dialogue scenarios (Zhang et al. 2025a), emotional scores generated by the agent exhibited a strong Pearson correlation (r=0.82r=0.82) with independently evaluated scores based on the Barrett–Lennard Relationship Inventory (BLRI), and also showed a high correlation (r=0.79r=0.79) with utterance-level empathy indicators, validating the psychological fidelity of this paradigm., to enable robust and reliable evaluation of OnlineMate’s educational effectiveness.

Figure 2 illustrates the workflow of the Evaluation Agent. Specifically, the workflow of the Evaluation Agent involves several key steps:

Role setting and scenario construction

The LLM is prompted to generate a specific student persona for the Evaluation Agent, including background information, personality traits, learning content, challenges faced in the learning process, goals, and expectations, thus simulating the diversity of real students’ experiences in learning. The learning content is selected from a content seed pool based on the actual classroom needs, while the student personality is chosen from a personality seed pool based on established classifications of student personality and cognition (Kagan 1966; Witkin et al. 1977).

Multi-turn dialogue simulation

The Evaluation Agent engages in multiple rounds of interaction within the OnlineMate system, simulating student behaviors such as questioning, thinking, and providing feedback during the learning process, with the aim of evaluating the quality of the system’s responses.

Emotional and cognitive evaluation and updating

After each dialogue round, the Evaluation Agent’s simulated student responses are evaluated according to Bloom’s Taxonomy to determine the cognitive level, and the agent’s psychological state and emotional changes are adjusted based on whether the system’s responses align with the student’s current challenges, intentions, and expectations. The agent’s ToM elements, including Belief, Desire, Intention, Emotion, and Thought, are updated, and the emotional support effectiveness of the system is scored. Through this comprehensive workflow, the Evaluation Agent is capable of thoroughly evaluating the OnlineMate system’s efficacy in fostering cognitive development and providing emotional support.

OnlineMate Agent

In the OnlineMate system, each OnlineMate Agent embodies a role defined by a specific persona, receiving student utterances as input, inferring the learner’s cognitive and psychological states through Theory of Mind (ToM), and generating responses aligned with its character.

Prior research has conceptualized the ToM reasoning process as a structured sequence of inference, beginning with the formulation of a set of plausible hypotheses regarding others’ mental states, followed by iterative testing and refinement of these hypotheses (Flavell 1979; Frith and Frith 2006; Grave de Peralta Menendez et al. 2008; Cross et al. 2024; Zhang et al. 2025b). Inspired by the human cognitive mechanism of employing ToM to infer others’ minds and generate appropriate responses, we decompose the OnlineMate Agent’s reasoning and response generation process into three stages: ToM hypothesis generation, hypothesis refinement and filtering, and response generation and validation. Figure 3 illustrates the complete workflow of OnlineMate Agents from obtaining input to generating responses.

ToM Hypothesis Generation

We initiate the OnlineMate Agent’s reasoning and response generation process with ToM Hypothesis Generation, which serves as the foundation for inferring students’ cognitive and psychological states. This process is grounded in the student’s current utterance, the dialogue context, and the agent’s memory of prior interactions.

Formally, given a student’s utterance at round rr, denoted as srs_{r}, the input to the OnlineMate Agent is represented as (sr,c​t​x<r,m​e​m<r)(s_{r},ctx_{<r},mem_{<r}), where c​t​x<rctx_{<r} captures the preceding dialogue history, and m​e​m<rmem_{<r} encodes dynamic memory reflecting the agent’s inferences about the student’s preferences, emotions, and other traits over time. The agent’s objective is to generate a set of candidate mental state hypotheses h1,h2,⋯,hk{h_{1},h_{2},\cdots,h_{k}}, each accompanied by a natural language explanation and a labeled ToM category from Belief,Desire,Intention,Emotion,Thought\textit{Belief},\textit{Desire},\textit{Intention},\textit{Emotion},\textit{Thought}. To ensure pedagogical relevance and prevent an overemphasis on psychological inference at the expense of instructional goals, we further incorporate reasoning about the student’s cognitive level, following the six-tier structure of Bloom’s Taxonomy (Muilenburg and Berge 2005; Apperly 2012), including Remember,Understand,Apply,Analyze,Evaluate,Create\textit{Remember},\textit{Understand},\textit{Apply},\textit{Analyze},\textit{Evaluate},\textit{Create}.

The ToM reasoning mechanism of the OnlineMate Agent unfolds in four stages: (1) initial hypothesis generation from (sr,c​t​x<r)(s_{r},ctx_{<r}) via LLM-based reasoning; (2) cross-referencing these hypotheses with m​e​m<rmem_{<r} to filter out implausible ones; (3) assigning each remaining hypothesis a corresponding ToM label; and (4) inferring the student’s current cognitive level based on the utterance srs_{r}. We design prompts that align with both psychological definitions of ToM and the levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy, guiding the LLM to reason about students’ mental and cognitive states in a manner analogous to human instructors. The resulting kk diverse and plausible hypotheses enable flexible downstream response generation, avoiding premature commitment to a single rigid response outline.

Hypothesis Refinement and Filtering

After inferring the student’s potential cognitive level and emotional state, OnlineMate Agents proceed to refine and filter these hypotheses to select those most aligned with the agent’s persona and the classroom instructional context for response generation. Unlike the previous stage, which primarily focused on inferring the student’s cognitive or affective state, the Hypothesis Refinement and Filtering step emphasizes evaluating the appropriateness of these hypotheses under broader constraints, such as the coherence with the agent’s persona and the dynamics of the ongoing classroom dialogue. This process ensures that OnlineMate Agents not only comprehend the learner’s state and intent but also respond in a manner that reflects character-consistent reasoning and behavior within a realistic educational setting.

The Hypothesis Refinement and Filtering stage takes as input the set of potential mental state hypotheses h1,h2,⋯,hk{h_{1},h_{2},\cdots,h_{k}} generated in the ToM Hypothesis Generation phase, along with constraint rules (role,c)(\textit{role},\textit{c}), which include the persona constraint role of the OnlineMate Agent and a set of contextual or normative constraints c that define specific behavioral guidelines or interpretive standards. These constraints serve as the basis for determining whether a given hypothesis should be retained, revised, or discarded. For example, if the initial hypothesis suggests that the student intends to play a game during a classroom dialogue, the rule-based constraints guide the OnlineMate Agent to reinterpret this intention in a contextually appropriate manner—such as treating it as an application scenario if the agent assumes the role of a teacher, or interpreting it as a playful remark if the agent is modeled as a student—thus ensuring alignment with both the agent’s persona and the instructional setting.

The Hypothesis Refinement and Filtering process is carried out in two sequential steps. First, for each initial hypothesis h1,h2,⋯,hkh_{1},h_{2},\cdots,h_{k}, the OnlineMate Agent generates a revised version h~i\tilde{h}_{i}, in which the original inference is reformulated to incorporate both persona constraints and contextual rule constraints. Subsequently, the agent evaluates each revised candidate h~i\tilde{h}_{i} by scoring it based on its plausibility, taking into account the current dialogue context and the agent’s memory. The most appropriate refined hypothesis, denoted as h~∗\tilde{h}^{*}, is then selected and passed on to the final stage for response generation and further validation.

Response Generation and Validation

In the final stage, the OnlineMate Agent generates an appropriate response and verifies its alignment with the inferred cognitive and psychological states of the student, transforming the refined hypothesis from the preceding stages into a concrete natural language output. This stage takes the selected hypothesis h~∗\tilde{h}^{*} as input. To ensure consistency with the student’s cognitive profile, prior emotional states, and the agent’s predefined persona, the response generation process incorporates memory m​e​m<rmem_{<r} and role constraints role, enabling the model to modulate the tone or structure of its response accordingly. Moreover, to steer responses toward enhancing the student’s cognitive level—a process termed “cognitive scaffolding”—the model is explicitly prompted to guide the student’s thinking through its answers. To further guarantee that the generated response aligns with the student’s inferred needs and intentions, a self-reflection mechanism is integrated into this process: the agent assigns a utility score to its own output, evaluating its usefulness in light of the known cognitive and affective states of the student, as well as its consistency with the conversational context and role-based constraints. If the utility score falls below a certain threshold, the system triggers a regeneration of the response to improve alignment and pedagogical effectiveness.

Experiments

Evaluation

We evaluate the effectiveness of the OnlineMate system using both automated and human evaluation methods. Unless otherwise specified, all reported evaluation results represent the average outcomes of 20 simulated classroom sessions conducted by the Evaluation Agent. These sessions were based on two courses: ”Digital Integrated Circuit Design” and ”Comprehensive Practice in Artificial Intelligence.” In each simulation, the number of dialogue turns is fixed at five, and the system includes four OnlineMate Agents, each assigned a distinct persona: a teacher with domain expertise, a student who is knowledgeable and actively participates, a student with partial understanding who only responds to familiar topics, and a student with limited foundational knowledge who faces learning difficulties.

Automated Evaluation

Automated evaluation leverages the Evaluation Agent to simulate student participation in OnlineMate-facilitated discussions and to score both cognitive engagement and emotional fluctuations throughout the learning process. For each dialogue turn, we prompt the LLM to analyze the Evaluation Agent’s utterance and assign a cognitive level score on a scale from 1 to 6, corresponding to Bloom’s Taxonomy, to assess whether OnlineMate Agents effectively facilitate cognitive advancement. Simultaneously, the Evaluation Agent—acting as a student—dynamically adjusts its emotional score based on the degree to which the OnlineMate Agents’ responses align with its psychological state and implicit intentions. If the emotional score falls below a predefined threshold, the dialogue is terminated. Emotional states are evaluated on a 0–100 scale, with each update occurring in increments of 5 points.

Human Evaluation

Human evaluation was conducted using standardized rubrics. Specifically, we adopted assessment scales developed by Carnegie Mellon University 22 2 https://www.cmu.edu/teaching/assessment/examples/courselevel-bycollege/cfa/tools/participationrubric-cfa.pdf and Northwestern University 33 3 https://searle.northwestern.edu/docs/assessment/discussion-rubric-examples.pdf to evaluate students’ performance in classroom discussions. These scales cover various dimensions, including frequency of participation, quality of comments, listening and co-construction, critical analysis, participation, and dialogue quality. Both the course instructor and educational experts were invited to independently rate each discussion segment, with a minimum of two experts assigned to each. The experts first assessed the plausibility and human-likeness of the Evaluation Agent’s simulated dialogue, and subsequently rated the dialogues that conformed to human student behavior based on the rubric criteria. All scores were mapped onto a 0–3 scale, and the average was then computed.

Results

Table 1 presents both automated and human evaluation results. From the automated evaluation, compared with a baseline multi-agent dialogue system, our OnlineMate system elevates the average cognitive level of student responses by one tier—shifting from slightly above Analyze to between Evaluate and Create. A similarly significant improvement is observed when compared with the OnlineMate variant lacking cognitive scaffolding, indicating that cognition-enhanced OnlineMate Agents effectively foster deeper learning and critical thinking, thereby stimulating students’ creative potential. Emotional scores also exhibit a marked increase, demonstrating that ToM-enhanced OnlineMate Agents are capable of accurately interpreting student intentions and engaging in communication that aligns more closely with learner expectations. The integration of cognitive-level inference and guidance further contributes to higher emotional scores, suggesting that the pursuit of advanced cognitive engagement is psychologically congruent with students’ intrinsic learning motivations. These findings not only affirm the pedagogical efficacy of OnlineMate but also validate the reliability and representativeness of the Evaluation Agent as a proxy for human learners.

Human evaluation further corroborates these findings, with our approach consistently achieving higher rubric scores than the baseline system. Interestingly, in the absence of cognitive enhancement, simulated students guided solely by ToM exhibit more attentive and engaging behavior during discussions. This is likely because responses generated without cognitive scaffolding tend to align more with students’ preferences, thereby encouraging further interaction and expression—albeit with limited contribution to cognitive advancement.

Further Analysis

The Number of Discussion Rounds

Figure 4 illustrates the average cognitive level exhibited in student utterances across 20 instructional and discussion sessions facilitated by OnlineMate, measured at varying dialogue turns. The cognitive score, ranging from 1 to 6, corresponds to the six hierarchical levels of Bloom’s Taxonomy, from Remember to Create. Our analysis reveals that at the onset of the sessions, students’ cognitive engagement demonstrated an upward trajectory, rising from an initial score of 3.4—positioned between Apply and Analyze—to a peak of 5.2, situated between Evaluate and Create. However, additional dialogue turns beyond this point did not yield further improvements in cognitive expression; instead, the cognitive level fluctuated within the Apply to Evaluate range. This suggests that while well-structured, in-depth discussions within OnlineMate can effectively elevate students’ cognitive engagement with a given topic, prolonged discourse on a single issue may lead to diminishing returns. Therefore, it is pedagogically advisable to conclude discussions at an optimal juncture, typically after five rounds, and transition to new learning content to sustain cognitive advancement.

The Number of Agents

Figure 5 illustrates the impact of varying the number of OnlineMate Agents on the highest cognitive level attained by students. As the teaching assistant role transitions from a single agent to multiple agents engaged in classroom discussions, a noticeable improvement in students’ highest cognitive levels is observed, highlighting the effectiveness and necessity of multi-agent discussions. However, when the number of agents exceeds four, the increase in cognitive level begins to plateau, and a decline is even noted when the number of agents surpasses six. This suggests that, in online learning contexts, an excessive number of agent companions may not necessarily be beneficial. An overabundance of agents providing excessive information may lead to cognitive overload, hindering the students’ learning process.

Conclusion

This paper presents OnlineMate, a multi-agent learning companion system based on LLMs and enhanced by ToM capabilities. The system not only simulates peer-like interactions but also dynamically adapts its interaction strategies based on learners’ cognitive and psychological states. This personalized pedagogical approach fosters a more engaging and reflective learning experience, promoting the development of higher-order thinking skills and emotional investment. Our evaluation results demonstrate that OnlineMate significantly enhances students’ cognitive engagement and facilitates more meaningful interactions, ultimately improving learning outcomes. The experimental findings further provide deeper insights into the mechanisms of AI-mediated learning. We envision that OnlineMate holds great promise for broader educational applications, serving as a powerful enabler of personalized learning experiences.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
